unit.title: Perform basic welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW) - fuel gas welding

summary: This unit teaches you to weld thin mild steel sheet safely with the oxy-acetylene flame, the oldest of the fuel gas welding processes. You will learn to handle and store gas cylinders, assemble and leak-test a welding set, light the torch and set the three flames, and make fusion runs, butt joints and outside corner joints by the leftward method. You will also learn to check and test your welds, deal with a backfire or flashback, shut the set down and report faults.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches the basic skills of **oxy-acetylene welding (OAW)**: working safely with gas cylinders, setting up and testing the equipment, lighting the torch, setting the right flame, and welding thin mild steel sheet, then checking your work and shutting down safely.

In oxy-acetylene welding, **oxygen** and **acetylene** gas are mixed in a torch and burned at a nozzle. The flame is hot enough to melt steel. You melt the edges of the joint into a **weld pool** and add metal from a **filler rod** where it is needed. No electricity is used, so a gas set can work where there is no power supply. In Jamaican workshops the same equipment is used for welding thin sheet, heating, bending, brazing and, with a cutting attachment, flame cutting: auto body and exhaust repairs, sheet-metal work, burglar-bar repairs and farm jobs.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, starting out in gas welding. You will work mostly on mild steel sheet about 1–2 mm thick, laid flat on firebricks. Welding in other positions, pipe, cast iron and braze welding come in the advanced oxy-acetylene unit.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely with gases
Know the dangers of oxygen and acetylene, wear the right PPE, keep the area clear of anything that burns, and know what to do in an emergency.
Handle and store cylinders
Move cylinders on a trolley, keep them upright and chained, and store them correctly.
Assemble and test the set
Fit regulators, flashback arrestors, hoses, check valves and torch the right way round, set working pressures, and leak-test every joint.
Light up and set the flame
Purge the hoses, light the fuel gas first with a spark lighter, and set a neutral, carburising or oxidising flame.
Prepare the job
Read the job sheet, choose the nozzle and filler rod, clean the edges, set the gap and tack the sheets.
Weld thin sheet
Make fusion runs with and without filler rod, and butt and outside corner joints by the leftward method.
Check and test welds
Inspect the face and the back of a weld, name the faults and their causes, and carry out a simple bend test.
Shut down, look after the gear and report
Shut the set down in the right order, bleed the hoses, clean nozzles, store everything safely and report faults.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on safety, cylinders, equipment, lighting up, flames, technique, joints, faults and shutting down.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: assembling and leak-testing a set, showing the three flames, making fusion runs on 1.6 mm sheet, and welding butt and outside corner joints that are then bend-tested. The assessor watches how you work, not only the finished weld.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms in the Revision section. Short-answer questions ask for exact trade words such as inner cone, spark lighter, working pressure gauge, tip cleaner, non-return valve and adjusting screw.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Oxy-acetylene welding has its own hazards. The flame is about **3100–3200 °C** at its hottest point, the gases are stored at high pressure, acetylene burns very easily, and oxygen makes everything else burn faster. Many gas welding accidents come from leaks, oil or grease on oxygen fittings, careless lighting, and cylinders that are knocked over.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Fire and explosion
Acetylene mixed with air burns or explodes from a tiny spark, over a very wide range of mixtures. A leak can fill a corner, a pit or a car body with gas that explodes when the torch is lit.
Leak-test every joint before lighting up
Fit flashback arrestors and check valves
Clear anything that burns; keep an extinguisher at hand
Never weld near cylinders, fuel or paint
Oxygen enrichment
Oxygen does not burn by itself, but air with extra oxygen in it makes clothes, hair and skin catch fire easily and burn fiercely. Oil and grease can catch fire on their own in pure oxygen.
Never use oxygen to blow dust off clothes or to freshen the air
Keep oil and grease off oxygen cylinders, valves, regulators and hoses
Never handle oxygen fittings with greasy gloves
Burns
The flame, the hot sheet, the filler rod and sparks burn. Hot steel looks the same as cold steel once it stops glowing.
Leather gloves, cotton overalls with long sleeves, safety boots
Tongs or pliers for hot work
Mark hot work HOT
Eye damage
The pool and the flame give off a bright glare and infrared rays that can damage your eyes over time. Sparks and hot metal can fly into them.
Gas welding goggles or a visor with a tinted filter, about shade 4 to 6
Clear safety glasses when chipping, cutting and wire brushing
Fumes
Heating paint, oil, zinc (galvanising) or plastic coatings gives off harmful fumes. Zinc fume causes metal fume fever.
Clean the metal first
Good ventilation; keep your head out of the fumes
Respirator when your instructor says
High-pressure cylinders
A cylinder that falls can break its valve. Gas escaping at full pressure can throw the cylinder like a rocket.
Cylinders upright and chained
Moved only on a trolley with the valves shut
Valve caps or guards fitted when moving
Sharp sheet
Cut sheet and offcuts have edges like a knife.
Gloves when handling sheet
Deburr edges
Offcuts straight into the scrap bin

head: PPE
Why
Check
rows: Gas welding goggles or visor, about shade 4–6
Cuts the glare and infrared light from the pool and flame, and keeps sparks out of the eyes
Filter not cracked
Clear cover lens not pitted
Strap holds them firmly
Leather gloves (gauntlets)
Heat, sparks and hot rod ends
Dry, free of oil and grease
No holes
Cotton or wool overalls, long sleeves
Sparks and heat on the skin
No oil or grease on them
Cuffs and collar buttoned; pockets closed
Safety boots
Falling sheet, cylinders and hot metal
Trouser legs worn over the boots
Cap
Sparks on the head and hair
Flame-resistant material

blocks.note: Arc welding helmets with shade 10–13 filters are too dark for gas welding: you cannot see the pool. Sunglasses and clear glasses give no protection from the glare. The shade you need depends on the size of the flame: about 4 to 6 for thin sheet, darker for heavy heating. Follow your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat tempts people to weld in a vest or a polyester sports shirt. Do not. Nylon and polyester melt onto the skin, and bare arms burn. Wear cotton, drink water often and take short breaks out of the heat. Take lighters and matches out of your pockets before you weld.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Weld on **firebricks** on a steel-topped bench, never on wood.
Clear away anything that can burn for about 10 metres: rags, paper, wood, paint tins, fuel. Cover what cannot be moved with a fire-resistant blanket.
Keep the cylinders well away from the flame, sparks and hot work, and keep hoses out of walkways and away from hot metal.
Keep a suitable fire extinguisher (for example dry powder or carbon dioxide) within reach.
Read the **safety data sheet (SDS)** for each gas. The gas supplier provides it: it gives the hazards, how to handle and store the gas, first aid and fire-fighting.
After welding, check the area for smouldering for at least 30 minutes, or longer if the workplace's rules say so.

head: What happens
What to do
rows: A spark or hot metal in the eye
Do not rub it. Rinse the eye gently with clean water or the eyewash station for several minutes, then get first aid and medical help.
A burn
Cool it under cool running water for about 20 minutes. Do not burst blisters or put butter, oil or toothpaste on it. Cover it loosely with a clean dressing and get first aid.
Clothes on fire
Stop, drop and roll, or smother the flames with a fire blanket. Cool the burn and call for help.
A fire at a hose or a leak that has caught light
If you can do it safely, close the cylinder valves. Use the extinguisher on burning materials. Raise the alarm.
An acetylene cylinder gets hot or catches fire
Clear everyone out of the area, raise the alarm and call the fire service (in Jamaica dial 110). Tell them an acetylene cylinder is involved. Do not try to move it.

blocks.note: Report every accident, burn, eye injury and near miss to your instructor, so it is recorded and the cause is put right.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Point
Oxygen
Acetylene
rows: What it does
Makes the acetylene burn much hotter than it would in air. Does not burn itself, but makes other things burn fiercely.
The fuel gas. Burns with oxygen to give the hottest flame of the common fuel gases.
Smell
None, so you cannot tell when the air has extra oxygen in it
A strong garlic-like smell, which helps you notice a leak
How it is stored
As a compressed gas at very high pressure, about 150–200 bar (over 2 000 psi) when full
**Dissolved in acetone**, which is soaked into a **porous filling** inside the cylinder, at a much lower pressure
Special dangers
Oil and grease can catch fire in pure oxygen
Unstable as a free gas above about 1 bar (100 kPa, 15 psi): never use it at a higher working pressure
Forms an explosive compound with copper
Hose colour
Blue (green on some American sets)
**Red**
Thread on fittings
Right-hand (tightens clockwise)
**Left-hand** (tightens anticlockwise); the nuts usually have a groove cut round their corners

blocks.note: Never let acetylene pass through copper pipe or through fittings with a lot of copper in them (above about 65–70%). Acetylene and copper form **copper acetylide**, which can explode from a knock or a little heat. Brass fittings made for acetylene are safe because they contain less copper.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Cylinder colours are not the same with every supplier or in every country, and old paint fades in the sun. **Read the name of the gas on the cylinder label**; never go by the colour alone.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Why the acetylene cylinder stays upright

blocks.p: The acetone that holds the acetylene is a liquid. If the cylinder lies down, acetone can flow out with the gas into the regulator and hoses. It damages the rubber and the regulator and spoils the flame. So an acetylene cylinder is always used and stored **upright**. If one has been lying down, for example on a delivery truck, stand it upright and leave it for the time the supplier gives before you use it.

Acetylene can only be drawn out of a cylinder at a limited rate, because the gas has to come out of the acetone. A very large nozzle can draw it too fast and pull acetone out with it. The supplier gives the safe rate; for big heating jobs, ask your instructor.

ul: Keep cylinders **upright and chained** or strapped to a wall, rack or trolley, so they cannot fall.

Move them on a proper cylinder **trolley**, chained, with the valves closed and the caps or guards fitted. Never roll them along the floor, drag them, or lift them by the valve, the cap or the regulator.
Never drop cylinders or let them bang together. Never use a cylinder as a roller or a support for work.
Keep them away from heat, flames, sparks and electric cables. Never let a welding arc touch a cylinder.
Close the cylinder valves when the set is not in use, and when a cylinder is empty. Mark empties EMPTY or MT and keep them apart from full ones.
Never try to repair a cylinder valve, change the markings or fill one cylinder from another. Faulty cylinders go back to the supplier.
Store them upright and secured in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place, out of direct sun and away from heat and anything that burns.
Keep oxygen apart from acetylene and other fuel gases, by a safe distance (often about 6 metres) or a fire-resistant wall, as the Centre's rules say, so that a fire at one is not fed by the other.
Keep full and empty cylinders apart and labelled.
Keep no oil, grease, paint or rags in the cylinder store, and display NO SMOKING signs.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's sun a cylinder left on an open truck or against a zinc fence gets very hot, and its pressure rises. Keep cylinders in shade, and on site keep them on the trolley in the shade, well away from the work.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The welding set and how to assemble it

blocks.p: An oxy-acetylene welding set has two cylinders, each with its own regulator, flashback arrestor and hose, joined at the torch. Every part on the acetylene side has left-hand threads, so the oxygen and fuel gas fittings cannot be mixed up.

head: Part
Its job
Check before use
rows: Cylinder valve
Opens and closes the cylinder. Some acetylene valves need a key (spanner), which is left on the valve while you work so it can be closed quickly.
Outlet clean, free of oil, grease and damage
Opens and closes smoothly
Regulator

Lowers the high cylinder pressure to a steady, low **working pressure**, and keeps it steady as the cylinder empties. Turning the **adjusting screw** in raises the working pressure; turning it out shuts the flow.
Gauge glasses not cracked, needles not bent or stuck
Threads and seat undamaged
Adjusting screw wound out before the cylinder valve is opened
Cylinder (contents) gauge
Shows the pressure in the cylinder. On oxygen it shows roughly how full the cylinder is.
Reads zero when the gas is off
Working pressure gauge
Shows the pressure going out to the hose. Also called the outlet, delivery or low-pressure gauge.
Reads zero when the hose is bled
Flashback arrestor
Stops a flame travelling back through the hose into the regulator and cylinder. It also stops gas flowing back. Fitted at the outlet of **both regulators**, and often at the torch as well.
Fitted to the right gas, flow arrow the right way
Not damaged; replaced or tested as the maker says
Hoses
Carry the gases to the torch: red for acetylene, blue for oxygen.
No cuts, cracks, burns, bulges or worn ends along the whole length
Clips or crimped ends secure
Never repaired with tape
Non-return (check) valves
Fitted where the hoses join the torch. They stop gas flowing backwards up the hose, for example oxygen being pushed into the acetylene hose.
Fitted the right way round on the right gas
Torch (blowpipe)
Has a valve for each gas and a mixer, where the gases are mixed before they reach the nozzle.
Valves close fully without forcing
No damage to the body or the seats
Nozzle (tip)
Its hole size controls the size of the flame. Chosen from the **maker's chart** for the metal and its thickness.
Hole round and clean, not blocked with spatter
Seat undamaged; screwed in firmly by hand or as the maker says

flow: Check both cylinders are chained upright on the trolley, are the right gases, and have clean valve outlets with no oil or damage
Fit the oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and the acetylene regulator (left-hand thread); tighten them with the right spanner, never with pliers and never by force
Fit a flashback arrestor to each regulator outlet
Check the hoses along their whole length, then connect them: red hose to acetylene, blue to oxygen
Fit the non-return valves and the torch, then the nozzle chosen from the maker's chart
Check the regulator adjusting screws are wound out (loose)
Stand to one side of the regulator, not in front of the gauges, and open each cylinder valve slowly
With the torch valves closed, turn each adjusting screw in to the working pressure on the chart
Brush leak-detection solution on every joint, from the cylinder valve to the nozzle, and watch for bubbles
Fix any leak with the gas turned off; test again; then purge each hose

blocks.note: Stand to the side when you open a cylinder valve. If a regulator is faulty, a sudden rush of high-pressure gas can burst the gauge glass and blow it out towards anyone standing in front. Open the valve **slowly**. Open a key-operated acetylene valve only about 1½ turns at most and leave the key on it, so it can be shut at once in an emergency.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Test for leaks with a leak-detection solution made for gas equipment, or soapy water if the Centre allows it. **Never** look for a leak with a flame, and never try to cure a leak by over-tightening a fitting or wrapping it in tape. A leak that will not stop means the part is faulty: tag it and report it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Choosing the nozzle and setting the pressures

blocks.p: The nozzle size and the working pressures go together. Both come from the **torch maker's chart**: find the metal and its thickness, read off the nozzle size, then set the oxygen and acetylene pressures the chart gives for that nozzle. A bigger nozzle gives a bigger, hotter flame for thicker metal. Nozzle numbers are not the same from one maker to another, so always use the chart for your own torch.

head: The chart tells you
Example for thin mild steel sheet (follow your own chart)
rows: Metal thickness
About 1–2 mm
Nozzle size
One of the smallest nozzles made for the torch
Working pressures
Low: often about 0.15–0.3 bar (about 2–4 psi, 15–30 kPa); on many torches both gases are set the same
Filler rod
Copper-coated mild steel rod, often 1.6 mm for 1.6 mm sheet

blocks.note: Gauges may read in bar, kilopascals (kPa) or pounds per square inch (psi). 1 bar = 100 kPa, which is about 14.5 psi. Read which scale your gauge uses before you set it. The acetylene working pressure must never go above 1 bar (15 psi).
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Lighting up and setting the flame

blocks.p: Before you light up, **purge** each hose: open one torch valve for a few seconds to let gas flow through, then close it, then do the same for the other gas. This clears out any air or mixed gas left in the hoses. Mixed gas in a hose can burn back into the hose when you light the torch. Purge in a well-ventilated place, away from any flame, and never purge both gases at the same time.

flow: Check the nozzle and the working pressures, and purge the hoses
Put on your goggles and gloves; point the torch away from people, the cylinders, the hoses and anything that can burn
Open the acetylene torch valve a little and light it at once with a **spark lighter**
Open the acetylene a little more, until the flame stops giving off black smoke
Slowly open the oxygen torch valve: a bright inner cone appears with a white feather round it
Keep adding oxygen until the feather just disappears into a clear, rounded inner cone: this is a **neutral flame**

blocks.note: Always light the **fuel gas first**, on its own, and only with a spark lighter. Never light a torch with matches or a cigarette lighter: your hand is too close to the nozzle, and a lighter can burst. Never light it from hot metal or from another torch.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Part
What it is
rows: Inner cone
The small, bright, sharp cone at the nozzle, where the oxygen and acetylene burn first
Hottest point
Just in front of the tip of the inner cone: about 3100–3200 °C in a neutral flame. This is the part you weld with.
Outer envelope
The larger, pale blue flame round the cone, where the rest of the gas burns with oxygen from the air. It shields the weld pool from the air.

head: Flame
Gas mixture
How it looks and sounds
Used for
rows: **Neutral**
About equal amounts of oxygen and acetylene
Clear, rounded inner cone with no feather; burns quietly
Welding mild steel and most general work. It adds nothing to the metal and takes nothing away.
**Carburising** (reducing)
Extra acetylene
A white **feather** round and beyond the inner cone; the longer the feather, the more extra acetylene
Only special jobs, such as hard-facing. On mild steel it adds carbon to the weld, making it hard and brittle.
**Oxidising**
Extra oxygen
Short, sharp, pointed inner cone, often a little purple; burns with a loud hiss
Not used on steel. A slightly oxidising flame is used with brass and bronze rods.

blocks.note: Set the flame by eye against the feather: start with a carburising flame and add oxygen until the feather just goes. If you add too much, turn the oxygen back until the feather just shows, then add a touch again. Check the flame often while you weld, because it can drift as the nozzle heats up or the cylinder pressure falls.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: What the wrong flame does to the weld

ul: **Oxidising flame on mild steel:** the pool sparks and foams, the steel burns, and the weld is brittle and full of holes.
**Carburising flame on mild steel:** the pool boils and looks dull, carbon is added, and the weld is hard and brittle.
**Neutral flame:** the pool is bright, clean and quiet, and flows smoothly.

blocks.p: With a neutral flame no **flux** is needed on mild steel: the outer envelope keeps the air off the pool. Flux is needed for other metals, such as cast iron and aluminium, and for brazing.

Close the torch valves in the order the torch maker and the Centre's rules give. Many makers say close the acetylene first, then the oxygen, because that puts the flame out cleanly without soot or a pop. Hang the torch up away from the cylinders, never on the regulators, and never leave a lit torch lying down.

head: Point
Backfire
Flashback (and sustained backfire)
rows: What happens
A loud **pop** as the flame snaps back into the nozzle. The flame goes out, or lights again by itself.
The flame burns back **inside the torch**, and in a flashback it travels up the hose towards the regulator and cylinder. Very dangerous.
Signs
A sharp crack or pop; a shower of sparks at the nozzle
A **squeal or hiss** from the torch, smoke or sparks at the nozzle, and the handle getting hot
Usual causes
Nozzle touching the work or the weld pool
Nozzle overheated, dirty or blocked with spatter
Working pressures too low
Loose nozzle
Wrong pressures
Hoses not purged, so mixed gas was in them
A leak, or a blocked nozzle
Arrestors or check valves missing or faulty
What you do
Shut the torch valves. Let the nozzle cool, clean it with a tip cleaner, check it is tight and the pressures are right, then relight.

Shut the torch valves **at once** (usually the oxygen first, then the acetylene, as the maker says), then close both cylinder valves. Tell your instructor. The torch, hoses and arrestors must be checked before the set is used again.

blocks.note: If a cylinder gets hot after a flashback or a fire, do not touch it. Clear the area, raise the alarm and call the fire service.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Read the **job sheet** before you start. It tells you the metal, its thickness, the joint, the size of the job and how it is to be welded. From the thickness you choose the nozzle, the pressures and the filler rod.

head: Joint
How the sheets meet
Notes for gas welding
rows: Butt joint
Edge to edge, in the same flat line
Square edges, touching or with a small gap, as the instructor directs
Outside corner joint
Two edges meet to make an L, with the corner on the outside
The edges melt together easily; little filler is needed
Flanged (edge) joint
Both edges are turned up and meet
Used on very thin sheet, under about 1.5 mm: the flanges melt down to form the weld, usually without filler, so burn-through is less likely
Lap joint
One sheet overlaps the other
The edge of the top sheet is welded to the face of the bottom sheet
Tee joint
One sheet stands on the face of the other
A fillet weld in the corner; needs more heat because the heat flows into two sheets

blocks.p: Gas welding mild steel uses **copper-coated mild steel filler rod**. The thin copper coating stops the rod rusting while it is stored; it does not act as a flux. Rods usually come in lengths of about 1 metre and in sizes such as 1.6 mm, 2.4 mm and 3.2 mm. A thicker sheet needs a thicker rod. Keep rods dry and clean, and never use rusty or oily rod.

flow: Mark out and cut the sheets to size; remove burrs with a file
Clean the edges and about 25 mm each side to bright metal: no rust, mill scale, paint, oil or dirt
Lay the sheets on firebricks, lined up, with the gap the instructor gives
Tack each end, then add tacks at even spacing along the joint (often about every 40–50 mm on thin sheet)
Check the sheets are level with each other and the gap is still even

blocks.note: Thin sheet moves as it heats. Without tacks the edges can close up, open out or ride over each other ahead of the weld. Short, close tacks hold the gap and stop the edges moving. Make each tack small and well fused, so the weld can melt it in.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Dirt, paint, oil and rust burn in the flame and leave **porosity** (gas holes) and poor fusion. The flame does not clean the joint for you.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Welding thin sheet: the leftward method

blocks.p: On thin steel, up to about 6 mm, the usual method is **leftward welding**, also called forehand welding. A right-handed welder holds the torch in the right hand and the filler rod in the left, starts at the right-hand end of the joint and works towards the left.

head: Point
Leftward (forehand) method
rows: Direction of travel
Right to left for a right-handed welder
Flame
Points **forward**, in the direction of travel, towards the part of the joint not yet welded, so it preheats the edges ahead
Torch angle
About 60–70° to the sheet
Filler rod
Held **in front of the flame**, at about 30–40° to the sheet, and dipped into the front edge of the pool
Inner cone
Tip held about **2–3 mm** above the pool, never touching it
Movement
A slight side-to-side movement of the torch, so both edges melt evenly into the pool

blocks.p: The other method, **rightward** or backhand welding, works from left to right with the flame pointing back at the finished weld and the rod following behind the flame. It is used on thicker steel and is taught in the advanced gas welding unit.
A fusion run is a weld made by melting a line along a single sheet, with no filler. It teaches you to make and move a weld pool, before you add rod.

flow: Mark straight lines on the clean sheet with soapstone; lay it on firebricks
Light up, set a neutral flame and lower your goggles
Hold the cone tip 2–3 mm above the start of the line until a small, bright, shiny pool forms
Move along the line at a steady speed with a slight side-to-side movement, keeping the pool the same size
Watch the pool: if it grows and sinks, move faster or lower the torch angle; if it will not form, move slower
At the end, lift the flame away slowly so the pool does not freeze with a hole
Let the sheet cool, then check the run: even width on top and an even line of melting on the back

ul: Keep the hot end of the rod inside the **outer envelope** of the flame, so it is hot and shielded from the air.
**Dip** the rod into the front edge of the pool, then draw it back a little; repeat in a steady rhythm.
Let the pool melt the rod. Never melt the rod in the inner cone so that it drips onto the plate: drops on cold metal do not fuse.
Never push the rod onto cold metal ahead of the pool.
Keep the rod and the torch moving together, so the pool stays the same size and shape.

blocks.note: Never let the nozzle touch the pool or the sheet. Spatter and molten metal block the hole, the nozzle overheats, and it **backfires**.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Butt joints and outside corner joints

head: Point
Butt joint in 1.6 mm sheet
Outside corner joint
rows: Set-up
Sheets level on firebricks, edges touching or with a small gap, tacked at each end and along the joint
Sheets held at 90° (a jig or angle iron helps), the edges meeting along the corner, tacked at each end and along
Welding
Melt both edges into one pool before you add rod; keep the side-to-side movement small and even
Melt the two edges together along the corner; add only a little rod to give a slightly rounded corner
Good result
Even ripples on top; an even line of penetration along the back
Smooth, slightly rounded corner; melting seen inside the corner along its length
Watch for
Burn-through if the pool is too big; unfused edges if it is too small
Edges melting back and leaving a gap; too much rod piling on the corner

blocks.p: Never snatch the flame away at the end. Fill the **crater** by adding a little more rod, then lift the flame away slowly. An unfilled crater is thin and weak, and it can crack.

head: What you see
Likely cause
What to do
rows: The pool will not form, or the rod sits on top in blobs
Too little heat: nozzle too small, travel too fast, or cone too far away
Hold the flame until a pool forms; travel slower; check the nozzle size
The pool grows, sags and drops through
Too much heat: nozzle too big, travel too slow, or flame too steep
Travel faster, lower the torch angle a little, or change to a smaller nozzle
The pool sparks and foams
Oxidising flame
Reset the flame to neutral
The pool boils and looks dull, with a feather on the flame
Carburising flame
Add oxygen until the feather just disappears
One edge melts and the other does not
Flame aimed to one side
Aim the flame along the middle of the joint and move evenly side to side

blocks.note: Rest your forearm or hand on something steady, and get into a comfortable position before you start, so you can move along the whole joint without stopping.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Let the weld cool, then clean it with a wire brush. Inspect it by eye in good light, top and back. A good gas weld on thin sheet has:

ul: Even ripples, with a steady width and height along the whole length
Smooth blending into the sheet at both edges: no groove (undercut) and no metal lying unfused on the surface
An even line of **penetration** along the back of a butt joint, with no burn-through and no places where the edges did not melt
No holes, cracks or burnt, sparkly surface
A filled crater at the end
Sheets still flat and in line

blocks.h: Common faults in gas welds on thin sheet

head: Fault
What it looks like
Main causes
How to prevent it
rows: Burn-through
Holes melted right through the sheet
Nozzle too big
Travel too slow
Gap too wide
Nozzle from the chart
Steady, faster travel
Correct gap
Lack of fusion
Filler lying on the edges without melting into them
Nozzle too small
Travel too fast
Rod melted before the edges were molten
Flame aimed to one side
Form a pool on both edges before adding rod
Correct nozzle and speed
Incomplete penetration
The back of a butt joint shows the edges not melted through
Too little heat
Gap too small
Travel too fast
Correct nozzle, gap and speed
Oxidised, porous weld
Rough, burnt, sparkly surface with holes
Oxidising flame
Dirty sheet
Neutral flame, checked often
Clean to bright metal
Porosity
Small gas holes
Rust, paint, oil or zinc on the sheet
Wrong flame
Clean the joint
Neutral flame
Undercut
A groove melted along the edge of the weld and left unfilled
Too much heat
Poor torch angle
Too little rod at the edges
Correct nozzle and angle
Add rod at the edges
Excess penetration
Too much weld metal hanging below the joint
Too much heat
Gap too wide
Less heat; correct gap
Unfilled crater
A hollow at the end of the run
Flame snatched away at the end
Add rod to fill it; lift the flame away slowly
Distortion
Sheet buckled or pulled out of line
Too much heat
Too few tacks
Close, even tacks
Correct nozzle and steady speed

blocks.p: A bend test shows whether the weld has fused right through. It is a **destructive test**: the test piece is spoiled.

flow: Cut a strip about 25 mm wide across the weld, with the weld in the middle of the strip
Clamp it in the vice with the weld just above the jaws
Bend it over with a hammer so that the back (root) of the weld is on the outside of the bend and is stretched
Look at the outside of the bend

head: Result
What it shows
rows: Bends right over with no cracks
Good fusion and full penetration
Opens up along the root
The edges were not melted through: incomplete penetration or lack of fusion
Cracks at small holes
Porosity, often from dirt or an oxidising flame

blocks.note: Wear safety glasses when cutting and bending. Stand to the side of the vice: a strip can spring out or snap. Treat test pieces as hot, and pick them up with tongs.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Shutting down, care of equipment and reporting

blocks.h: Shutting down at the end of the day

flow: Put the flame out by closing the torch valves in the maker's order
Close both cylinder valves
Open the oxygen torch valve to bleed the oxygen hose until both oxygen gauges read zero, then close it
Do the same for the acetylene
Wind out both regulator **adjusting screws**, so no pressure is held on them
Coil the hoses loosely without kinks and hang them up, away from heat, oil and sharp edges
Let the nozzle cool, then clean it and put spare nozzles away in their box
Leave the cylinders chained upright on the trolley; check the area for anything smouldering

blocks.note: Bleeding the hoses means no gas is left under pressure in the hoses or regulators overnight. Never take a regulator off a cylinder while there is still gas in it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: If you stop welding for a few minutes, shut the torch off and hang it up away from the cylinders. Never leave a lit torch on the bench or hang it on a regulator or cylinder. For a longer break, close the cylinder valves too.

ul: Clean a dirty or blocked nozzle with a **tip cleaner** of the right size: push it straight in and out, without twisting hard, so the hole stays round and is not made bigger. A damaged nozzle gives a crooked flame and backfires.
Never use oil or grease on the torch, regulators, hoses or cylinder valves. Wipe them with a clean, dry cloth.
Keep hoses away from hot metal and sparks; do not let anyone drive or drop anything on them.
Keep spare nozzles, spanners and the spark lighter in their places, and replace a worn lighter flint.

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Faulty equipment
A leak that will not stop, a cut or burnt hose, a cracked gauge glass, a sticking needle, a gauge that does not read zero, a damaged nozzle seat
Stop using it, label it DO NOT USE or FAULTY, and tell your instructor. Never repair a regulator yourself.
Backfires and flashbacks
A flashback, or backfires that keep happening
Report it so the torch, hoses and arrestors are checked
Injuries and near misses
Burns, a spark in the eye, a small fire, a cylinder knocked over
Get first aid, and make sure it is recorded
Gas and materials
A cylinder nearly empty, rods running short, damp or rusty rods
Tell your instructor so stock is reordered

blocks.note: Training centres keep records of accidents, near misses and faulty equipment. Report at once, say exactly what happened, and fill in the job card or logbook for your work.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of oxy-acetylene welding and say how each one is controlled.
I can explain why oxygen must never be used to blow off clothes or freshen the air, and why oil must be kept off oxygen fittings.
I can choose and check PPE for gas welding, including goggles of about shade 4 to 6.
I can explain how acetylene is stored, why its cylinder stays upright, and why copper must not be used with it.
I can move, secure and store cylinders safely.
I can name the parts of the set and say what each does.
I can assemble the set, open the cylinder valves safely and leak-test every joint.
I can choose a nozzle and set the pressures from the maker's chart.
I can purge the hoses, light the torch fuel gas first, and set a neutral flame.
I can describe the neutral, carburising and oxidising flames and what each is used for.
I can explain the difference between a backfire and a flashback, and what to do for each.
I can prepare, gap and tack thin sheet for welding.
I can make fusion runs, butt joints and outside corner joints by the leftward method.
I can inspect a gas weld, name its faults with their causes, and carry out a bend test.
I can shut down the set, bleed the hoses, look after the nozzles and report faults.

terms: The liquid inside an acetylene cylinder that the acetylene is dissolved in
The fuel gas used in oxy-acetylene welding
The screw or knob on a regulator that sets the working pressure; wound out at shut-down
A pop as the flame snaps back into the nozzle
Letting the gas out of the hoses and regulators after the cylinder valves are closed
Two sheets meeting edge to edge in the same flat line
A flame with extra acetylene, showing a white feather
Two sheets meeting at their edges to make an L shape
The hollow left at the end of a run if it is not filled
The rod melted into the pool to add metal to the weld
The flame burning back inside the torch and up the hose
A safety device at the regulator (and often the torch) that stops a flashback reaching the cylinder
A run made by melting a line along the sheet without filler
The small, bright cone of flame at the nozzle
Welding from right to left with the rod in front of the flame; also called forehand
A flame with about equal oxygen and acetylene; used for mild steel
A valve at the torch that stops gas flowing backwards up the hose; also called a check valve
The end of the torch where the flame burns; its size is chosen from the maker's chart
A flame with extra oxygen; short, pointed cone and a hiss
The metal being welded, as opposed to the filler rod
How far the weld has melted through the joint
Small gas holes in the weld
Letting gas flow through each hose for a few seconds before lighting up
The device that lowers cylinder pressure to a steady working pressure
Welding from left to right with the rod following behind the flame; also called backhand
The supplier's sheet giving a gas's hazards, handling, first aid and fire-fighting
The flint lighter used to light the torch
A short weld that holds the parts in place before the full weld
A small file-like wire used to clean the hole of a nozzle
The pool of melted metal under the flame
The regulator gauge that shows the pressure going out to the hose

c1.title: A new set-up in the gas bay in Kingston
c1.text: Odane and Tishauna, trainees at a training centre in Kingston, are setting up a new oxy-acetylene set in the gas bay. The acetylene cylinder arrived an hour ago lying on its side on the back of the delivery truck. A greasy rag has been left draped over the oxygen regulator, and Odane notices a short crack near one end of the red hose. When the cylinder valves are opened, Tishauna brushes leak-test solution on every joint.

c2.title: Sheet-metal panels at a shop in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Javon works at a small sheet-metal shop in Ocho Rios, St Ann, welding 1.2 mm mild steel panels for a food cart. The sheets have light rust and an oily film. His first run sparked and foamed, and the finished weld looked rough and burnt. On his next run the flame showed a long white feather round the inner cone. On a third, the pool kept growing and dropping through the sheet, leaving holes.

c3.title: Pops and a squeal on a farm job in Santa Cruz
c3.text: Rushane is repairing a thin steel water trough on a farm near Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, with the farm's gas set. He rests his hand on the trough and the nozzle keeps touching the pool. The torch pops loudly several times and the flame goes out, then lights again. He carries on. Later he hears a squeal from the torch and feels the handle getting hot.

c4.title: Closing the gas bay in Old Harbour
c4.text: At 4:30 p.m. Kerry-Ann is asked to close down the gas welding bay at a fabrication shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine. The nozzle is still hot from the last job and its hole is partly blocked with spatter. When she bleeds the hoses, the needle on the acetylene working pressure gauge stays at 0.2 bar instead of falling to zero.

c5.title: Corner joints for planter boxes in Falmouth
c5.text: At a training centre in Falmouth, Trelawny, Sanjay is making small planter boxes from 1.6 mm mild steel sheet with outside corner joints, then testing a butt joint from the same sheet. On his first box he put one tack at each end of a 300 mm corner, and the edges opened out and rode over each other as he welded. His bend-test strip opened up along the back of the weld.

questions.q: What should be done with the acetylene cylinder before it is connected?
o: Lay it flat again so the gas comes out more smoothly
Stand it upright and wait as long as the supplier says
Roll it across the floor to mix the gas with the acetone
Connect it at once but open the valve only a quarter turn
questions.why: Lying down lets acetone run into the valve, and it can come out with the gas and damage the regulator and hoses. Stand the cylinder upright and wait as the supplier says before use.

questions.q: Why is the greasy rag on the oxygen regulator dangerous?
o: Grease makes the gauge needles stick so the pressure reads wrong
The rag stops the regulator from cooling down while gas flows
Oil and grease can catch fire on their own in pure oxygen
Grease softens the blue hose so that it bursts at the regulator
questions.why: Oil and grease can ignite by themselves in contact with high-pressure oxygen, starting a fierce fire at the regulator. Keep every oxygen fitting, and your gloves, free of oil and grease.

questions.q: What should Odane do about the crack near the end of the red hose?
o: Wrap the crack firmly with insulating tape and test it with solution
Use the set and keep the acetylene pressure low to protect the hose
Swap the red hose to the oxygen side, where the pressure is higher
Take the hose out of use, label it faulty and report it
questions.why: A cracked fuel hose can leak acetylene, which can explode or catch fire. Hoses are never repaired with tape: the damaged hose is tagged out and replaced.

questions.q: Tishauna's leak-test solution shows bubbles growing at the nut where the acetylene regulator joins the cylinder. What should they do?
o: Tighten the nut hard with pliers while the gas is still on
Shut off the gas, release the pressure, then re-make the joint
Wrap the joint in tape and test it once more before lighting
Carry on, since a small leak at the cylinder is quickly blown away
questions.why: Leaks are fixed with the gas turned off and the pressure released, using the right spanner, then tested again. A joint that still leaks means a faulty part, which is tagged and reported.

questions.q: What should Javon do to the sheets before he welds again?
o: Nothing, because the flame burns off rust and oil as it welds
Heat them red hot all over first to burn off the oily film
Paint the edges with flux so it can lift off the rust and oil
Clean the edges and the area beside them to bright metal
questions.why: Rust and oil burn in the flame and give porosity and poor fusion; the flame does not clean the joint. Clean the edges and about 25 mm each side to bright metal before welding.

questions.q: Which flame did Javon most likely use for his first, sparking run?
o: A neutral flame with the cone held too far from the pool
A carburising flame with a short white feather on it
An oxidising flame, with too much oxygen in the mixture
An acetylene-only flame with no oxygen added at all
questions.why: A pool that sparks and foams and leaves a rough, burnt weld is the sign of an oxidising flame. Turn the oxygen back until the feather just shows, then set the flame neutral.

questions.q: On his second run the flame shows a long white feather. What should he do?
o: Turn the acetylene up until the feather is longer and brighter
Carry on, because a feather gives a stronger weld on thin sheet
Turn both torch valves down to make the whole flame smaller
Add oxygen slowly until the feather just disappears
questions.why: A white feather means extra acetylene: a carburising flame, which adds carbon and makes the weld hard and brittle. Adding oxygen until the feather just goes gives a neutral flame.

questions.q: On the third run the pool keeps dropping through. Which change is most likely to cure it?
o: Use a bigger nozzle so the edges melt and fuse more quickly
Hold the inner cone right down in the pool to steady it
Travel faster, or fit a smaller nozzle from the chart
Turn the oxygen up until the flame starts to hiss loudly
questions.why: Holes come from too much heat: a nozzle too big for 1.2 mm sheet or travel that is too slow. A smaller nozzle from the chart, or a steadier, faster travel, keeps the pool small.

questions.q: What is causing the loud pops?
o: The nozzle touching the pool, overheating and blocking
The cylinders running low on acetone and oxygen
The filler rod being dipped into the front of the pool
The neutral flame being too hot for thin steel sheet
questions.why: A pop as the flame snaps back into the nozzle is a backfire. It is usually caused by the nozzle touching the work or pool, or by an overheated or blocked nozzle.

questions.q: After the pops, what should Rushane have done before carrying on?
o: Turned the working pressures up so the flame could not snap back
Shut the torch, let the nozzle cool, clean it and check it
Opened the oxygen valve wider to blow the spatter out of the hole
Changed to a larger nozzle that is harder to block with spatter
questions.why: Repeated backfires mean the nozzle is hot, dirty or touching the work. Shut off, cool and clean the nozzle with a tip cleaner, check it is tight and the pressures are right, then relight and keep the cone off the pool.

questions.q: When he hears the squeal and feels the handle getting hot, what must he do first?
o: Plunge the lit torch into a bucket of water to cool it
Pull the hoses off the torch so the flame cannot reach them
Shut the torch valves at once, then the cylinder valves
Keep the torch pointing down and wait for the noise to stop
questions.why: A squeal and a hot handle mean the flame is burning inside the torch and may be heading up the hose. Shut the torch valves at once (usually oxygen first, as the maker says), then both cylinder valves.

questions.q: After the squeal has been dealt with, what happens to the set?
o: It is used again once the torch has cooled enough to hold
It is used again after the nozzle is cleaned with a tip cleaner
It is used again if it lights up next time without a pop or squeal
It is not used until its torch, hoses and arrestors are checked
questions.why: A flashback can damage the torch, hoses, check valves and arrestors without it showing. The set is reported and checked by a competent person before it is used again.

questions.q: After closing both cylinder valves, what does Kerry-Ann do next?
o: Open each torch valve in turn to bleed it to zero, then close it
Unscrew both regulators so the gas left inside can escape slowly
Turn both adjusting screws fully in so they hold the gas in the hoses
Leave the hoses full of gas so that lighting up is quicker tomorrow
questions.why: Bleeding each hose through its torch valve until the gauges read zero leaves no gas under pressure overnight. Then the adjusting screws are wound out.

questions.q: Why does it matter that the nozzle hole is kept clean and round?
o: A blocked or damaged hole gives a crooked flame and backfires
A clean hole lets the cylinders empty much more slowly overnight
A round hole stops the hose from cracking where it joins the torch
A clean hole makes the flame cooler and much easier to look at
questions.why: Spatter in the hole, or a hole forced out of round, makes the flame crooked or unsteady and causes backfires. Clean it, when cool, with a tip cleaner of the right size pushed straight in and out.

questions.q: What should she do about the gauge that stays at 0.2 bar?
o: Tap the glass with a spanner until the needle falls back to zero
Note that it reads 0.2 bar high and take that off each reading
Tag the regulator out of use and report it to her supervisor
Turn the adjusting screw in and out until the needle moves
questions.why: With the hose bled, the gauge should read zero; a needle that stays up means the gauge or regulator is faulty, so its readings cannot be trusted. Label it faulty, stop using it and report it.

questions.q: How should Sanjay have tacked the 300 mm corner?
o: One tack in the middle only, so both ends were free to move
No tacks, holding the sheets steady with his gloved hand
Tacks at each end and then at even, close spacing along it
Two long tacks of about 50 mm, one at each end of the joint
questions.why: Thin sheet expands and moves as it heats. Small tacks at each end and then at short, even spacing (often about every 40–50 mm) hold the edges in line and the gap even.

questions.q: Sanjay's bend strip opened up along the back of the weld. What does this show?
o: The root did not melt through: incomplete penetration
The weld was much stronger than the sheet around it
The flame was neutral and the weld was sound throughout
The strip was cut too wide for the vice to bend it
questions.why: The root is on the outside of the bend, so any part of the joint that did not melt through opens up. More heat at the root, the right gap and a steady speed give full penetration.

questions.q: Which sign on the back of his next butt weld would show good penetration?
o: A dark, burnt band beside the joint with the edges still seen
An even, narrow line of melting along the whole length
Several small holes where the pool dropped through
A high, rounded bead on the top face and nothing below
questions.why: A sound butt weld in thin sheet shows an even line of penetration along the back, with no holes and no unmelted edges. The top alone does not tell you the weld has fused through.

questions.q: Why is a regulator's adjusting screw wound out before the cylinder valve is opened?
o: So full cylinder pressure does not slam into the regulator
So the cylinder gauge can show how much gas is left inside
So the hose fills with gas before the torch valves are opened
So the working pressure starts at its highest setting
questions.why: With the screw wound out, the regulator is closed. Opening the cylinder valve then cannot send a sudden rush of high-pressure gas through to damage the regulator, its gauges or the hose.

questions.q: Shanté has just lit the acetylene and it is burning with black smoke. What should she do next?
o: Open the oxygen valve fully at once to clear the smoke
Hold the nozzle against the firebrick to steady the flame
Turn off the acetylene and light the oxygen on its own
Open the acetylene a little more until the smoke stops
questions.why: After lighting, the acetylene is turned up a little until the flame stops smoking. Then oxygen is added slowly until the feather just disappears, giving a neutral flame.
